newsitem.title: HONG KONG: British leave HK legacy of tea, clubs, and cricket.
newsitem.headline: British leave HK legacy of tea, clubs, and cricket.

text.p: The British are leaving but they are leaving a lot behind.
Workmen are busy hauling away monarchical symbols of colonialism, the "royal" signs and crown insignia, to make way for Chinese rule under the five-starred red flag from July 1.

Dwarfed by Hong Kong's Manhattan-like array of glass and steel skyscrapers, some vintage remnants cling on -- ornate, pillared Victorian and Edwardian buildings, English-style parks with manicured lawns and bilingual signs.
This onetime barren, rocky territory that became a wealthy East Asian economic hub has seen relentess property development that obliterated many relics worthy of "heritage" preservation.

A cricket ground, where spectators once sipped brandy-and ginger ale in the heart of Hong Kong, fell victim to the advance of tower blocks and the club has transferred inland, pledging to spread the exotic game to local Chinese.
Traditions like cricket are reinforced by another English custom--exemplified by the daily rite of afternoon tea and cucumber sandwiches in the splendour of the Peninsula Hotel.
Another real legacy is Hong Kong's devotion to "rule of law", buttress of civil liberty, espoused by many legislators. Centuries-old English Common Law is the basis of Hong Kong's judicial system.
Civil servants in the new era as a Special Administrative Region of China are set to play down honours from Queen Elizabeth like "Sir" titles in a knighthood.

And private clubs, once an all-male British legacy, are changing fast. The exclusive Hong Kong Club, long an enclosed bastion of colonialism -- a kind of imperial Jurassic Park to some citizens -- has decided to admit women as members.

Another bastion, the Royal Hong Kong Yacht Club (patron Queen Elizabeth), became a rarity by retaining the 100-year-old "royal" title but found an ingenious answer-- dropping "royal" in the Chinese title.

The death of empire brings a legacy likely to endure for some time, maybe generations. Many symbols of the 156-year colonial rule cannot be removed or taken home when Britain departs and China takes over on Monday night.
Hong Kong's bustling streets are studded with signs bearing the names of former colonial governors -- Pottinger, Macdonnell, Kennedy, Nathan, Bowen, Robinson.

An exceptional absence is the 28th and final Governor, Chris Patten, a career-politician who leaves town next Monday night after a five-year stint marked by a meet-the-people style that won wide popularity. But China disliked his democracy reforms.
Main thoroughfares bear the hallmarks of royalty -- Queen's Road, King's Road, Queen Victoria Street. A principal wharf is called Queen's Pier. A top garrison is Prince of Wales Barracks.
Muse Cheung, environmental and leisure officer of the Urban Council which runs metropolitan Hong Kong, said her department generally does not plan to change colonial street names.
One exception though is Victoria Park, named after the Empress Queen when a naval landing party planted the Union Jack flag on Hong Kong Island's Possession Point in January 1841.
The Urban Council said it has no plans to remove her statue after the handover. It has been restored after an eccentric Chinese sculptor vandalised it with red paint.

Victoria Park, likely to be renamed Hong Kong Central Park, is the venue of an annual pro-democracy, candle-lit vigil honouring people killed in China's bloody 1989 anti-democracy crackdown. Some 55,000 people joined the vigil this June 4.

Hong Kong is dotted with eye-catching examples of colonial architecture. The 150-year-old St John's Cathedral in the downtown Central area, the former French Mission Building on Battery Path, the harbour-front Clock Tower, will all be reminders of Britain's century and a half in Hong Kong.

A colossal landmark of British rule is emerging in the imperial twilight and it has no colonial name. One of the world's biggest construction projects is the $US20 billion new international Chek Lap Kok airport, named after an island flattened to build it, and the associated Tsing Ma bridge, the world's largest combination road-rail suspension link.
